findings.text: The Lua long-string fence `{ mark: '=', open: '[', close: ']', suffix: ']' }` has no `prefix: '['`. `fenceAt` (src/count.ts:186-189) counts marks from `i` and then looks for `open` at the end of the run. With no prefix and zero marks, the `[` at `i` passes as its own `open`. So every single `[` opens a long string closed by `]]`, and the string runs on over lines. For example, `t[1] = 2` / `-- note` / `x = 1` counts the comment line as code until some `]]` turns up; `{[k] = v}` and `a[b]` do the same. `[==[ … ]==]` also opens at its first `[` with closer `]]` instead of `]==]`, so `local s = [==[` / `]]` / `-- inside` / `]==]` counts line 3 as a comment. The `=` rule for long strings is not met. Fix: add `prefix: '['` (specialsOf still picks `[`).

The Lua long-string test can't catch the bug above. Every line is code no matter how strings are read: `[==[` actually closes early at the `]]` on line 2, and `t[1][2]` opens a long string that never closes, but the expected counts still come out the same. Add a line that is a comment only when the long string is read right, e.g. `]]` then `-- x` inside a `[==[` string, or a comment line after `t[1]`.

This test passes even without the raw-identifier and word-prefix checks. `let r#type = bar; // x` and `let fooBr#"x"# = 1;` are code however `r`/`#`/`"` are read, so removing the `\w` check at src/count.ts:185 fails nothing. It needs a case where opening a raw string by mistake changes a count, e.g. `let fooBr#"x = 1; // "` followed by a `// c` line.

The byte-string test passes without `br`/`b` support: with plain `"` strings, every line is still code. It never checks that a `br#"…"#` holding `"` or `//` keeps a following comment line counted as a comment.

The escape test passes without escape handling. With no escapes, `\"` closes the string and `";` opens a new one, but both lines are still code. There is no comment line whose count depends on the escape.

The lifetime/label half of this test gives the same counts under the old rule, where `'` was a single-line string. Line 1 has three `'`, so the old rule opens a string to the end of the line, and that line is code anyway; the label line has two. A lifetime followed by a comment opener, e.g. `fn f(x: &'a str) {} /* open` / `still */`, is needed to show that `'` opens nothing.

The Swift raw-string test doesn't exercise the escape rule it names. On every line, the result is the same whether a plain `\` escapes, `\#` escapes, or nothing escapes, since no closer is ever preceded by `\` or `\#`. Cases like `#"a\"#` (a plain backslash does not escape, so the string closes) and `#"a\#"# still"#` (the escaped quote does not close) are missing.

blind.summary: Rust and Swift work for the cases the goal lists. Lua long strings are broken: the long-string fence is missing its `[` prefix, so every `[` in Lua code opens a string that only `]]` closes, and `[=[…]=]` is never read right. This bug undoes the goal for Lua and is easy to hit, since ordinary indexing like `t[1]` triggers it. The Lua long-string test misses it because every line it checks is code anyway. Several other new tests also give the same counts with or without the feature they name: Rust byte strings, Rust escapes, the raw-identifier/word-prefix case, Rust lifetimes vs. the old `'`-as-string rule, and the escapes in Swift raw strings. These are notes on the tests only; I found no code bug behind them.
